title: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
summary: Why each version exists, what problem it solved, and how to see which one you're using.

steps.title: HTTP/1.1 and head-of-line blocking
body: HTTP/1.1 sends text requests over TCP. **Keep-alive** reuses a connection for several requests, but **one at a time**: response 2 can't start until response 1 is done.
A slow response blocks everything behind it: **head-of-line blocking**.

Browsers work around it by opening **about 6 connections per host**, and sites used to *shard* assets across `img1.`, `img2.` hostnames and bundle files into sprites. Each extra connection costs its own TCP and TLS handshakes.

steps.prompt: A page loads 30 small images from one host over HTTP/1.1. Why is it slow even on a fast link?
options: At most ~6 requests are in flight at once, so it takes several round trips
TCP limits files to 6 per second
steps.explain: Latency, not bandwidth: 30 requests over 6 connections is 5 sequential rounds.

steps.title: HTTP/2: one connection, many streams
body: HTTP/2 keeps the same methods, headers and status codes, but changes the wire format:
- **multiplexing**: many requests (*streams*) interleaved over **one** TCP connection, so nothing waits for a slow response;
- **HPACK** header compression (cookies aren't re-sent in full each time);
- negotiated during TLS with **ALPN** `h2`. Browsers only do HTTP/2 over TLS.
What it couldn't fix: TCP itself delivers bytes in order, so **one lost packet stalls every stream** until it's retransmitted.

steps.prompt: This models a page with 12 resources on a 100 ms round trip, ignoring setup. What does it print?
code: int h1Rounds = (resources + 5) / 6;   // 6 connections, one request each at a time
int h2Rounds = 1;                     // all multiplexed at once

steps.title: HTTP/3: QUIC over UDP
body: HTTP/3 replaces TCP with **QUIC**, a transport built on **UDP**:
- each stream is delivered independently, so a lost packet only stalls **its own** stream;
- the transport and TLS 1.3 handshakes are **combined**: one round trip to a new server, zero (**0-RTT**) when resuming;
- connections survive **network changes** (Wi-Fi to mobile) because they're identified by a connection ID, not the IP/port pair.
A server advertises it with a header on an HTTP/2 response; the browser tries QUIC next time:
If UDP 443 is blocked by a firewall, browsers silently fall back to HTTP/2.

steps.prompt: Complete the commands: ask curl for HTTP/2 and show only headers, then show which protocol was used.
Match each symptom to the version detail behind it.
pairs: The site uses h2 over HTTPS, but plain `http://` requests to it always get HTTP/1.1
HTTP/2 is negotiated with ALPN inside the TLS handshake
HTTP/3 never used inside the office
Mobile call drops less when switching Wi-Fi to 4G
One lost packet stalls all images

steps.title: Model page load time
prompt: Write `int LoadTimeMs(string version, int resources, int rttMs)` with this simple model:
- **setup**: `"1.1"` and `"2"` pay 2 round trips (TCP + TLS 1.3); `"3"` pays 1 (combined QUIC handshake).
- **requests**: `"1.1"` needs `ceil(resources / 6)` rounds; `"2"` and `"3"` need 1 round (if `resources > 0`, else 0).
- total = (setup + request rounds) x `rttMs`. Any other version throws `ArgumentException`.
starter: int LoadTimeMs(string version, int resources, int rttMs)
solution: int LoadTimeMs(string version, int resources, int rttMs)
default: throw new ArgumentException("unknown version " + version);
hints: A `switch` on the version sets setup and rounds.

steps.title: Parse Alt-Svc
prompt: Write `List<(string Protocol, int Port)> ParseAltSvc(string header)`. Entries are comma-separated; each starts with `proto="host:port"` (host usually empty)
and may be followed by `; ma=...` parameters to ignore. `clear` alone means no alternatives (return an empty list).
starter: List<(string Protocol, int Port)> ParseAltSvc(string header)
solution: List<(string Protocol, int Port)> ParseAltSvc(string header)
var result = new List<(string Protocol, int Port)>();
foreach (var entry in header.Split(',', StringSplitOptions.TrimEntries | StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries))
template: Dojo.Eq("two entries", new List<(string Protocol, int Port)> { ("h3", 443), ("h3-29", 8443) }, ParseAltSvc("h3=\":443\"; ma=86400, h3-29=\":8443\""));
Dojo.Eq("with host", new List<(string Protocol, int Port)> { ("h2", 443) }, ParseAltSvc("h2=\"alt.example:443\""));
Dojo.Eq("clear", new List<(string Protocol, int Port)>(), ParseAltSvc("clear"));
hints: Split on `,`, then keep the part before the first `;`.
Split that at `=`, strip quotes, take the digits after the last `:`.
